implementation_notes: System.Linq's Enumerable.Aggregate is the runtime's fold with exactly three overloads - Aggregate(func), Aggregate(seed, func) and Aggregate(seed, func, resultSelector) - and it applies the accumulator function over any IEnumerable<T>, with deferred execution until the query is enumerated. The built-in aggregates (Sum, Min, Max, Average, Count, String.Concat/Join) are the monoid specializations, and they should be preferred where they apply because they are the implementations the BCL optimises and a hand-written Aggregate is not. For a recursive data type the BCL offers no catamorphism: that fold is written over the node type, most readably with the record-pattern switch of the sibling variant.
code_sketch:
var total = orders.Aggregate(0m, (sum, o) => sum + o.Amount);            // seed fold

var rounded = orders.Aggregate(
    0m,
    (sum, o) => sum + o.Amount,
    sum => Math.Round(sum, 2));                                          // + resultSelector

decimal same = orders.Sum(o => o.Amount);   // monoid specialization wins where it exists
pitfalls: Aggregate is left-associative and has no right-fold counterpart: a right-nesting combine needs Reverse() (which buffers the whole sequence) or a recursive function.

Deferred execution means the fold happens at enumeration time: folding the same query twice re-enumerates the source, so a single-use iterator or a streaming source is consumed once and then folds over nothing.

The seed-less overload throws InvalidOperationException on an empty sequence while the seeded overload silently returns the seed, which is correct only if the chosen seed is really the identity (0 is fine for sum, wrong for min).

variants.name: Recursive fold over a record hierarchy with property/positional patterns
variants.idiom_name: switch expression with property/positional patterns over sealed record cases
variants.implementation_notes: C# 8 and later turn the hand-written catamorphism into a readable one: model the cases as records (an abstract base plus one derived record per case), write the algebra as a switch expression matching property or positional patterns - the components then arrive as variables in the arm - and recurse from each arm. Pattern matching over a hierarchy is checked: the compiler reports warning CS8509 when a switch expression does not cover all possible values, so a new case is reported but not rejected, which means TreatWarningsAsErrors or an explicit reachable throw arm is what turns the warning into a build failure. Prefer this over a class-per-operation Visitor hierarchy when operations are few and cases change often; use a Visitor when operations multiply while cases stay fixed.
pitfalls: CS8509 is a warning, not an error: without TreatWarningsAsErrors a missing case ships and the discard arm becomes a runtime throw instead of a compile-time report.

Pattern matching recurses through the same call stack as any recursive method: a deeply nested record tree overflows the stack, and the CLR provides no tail-call guarantee for a fold that combines two children.

Records are reference types with structural equality, so using a record as the accumulator allocates one object per step; fold into a struct/primitive carrier or an in-place accumulator when the fold is hot.
